source.title: How Well Do Large-Scale Chemical Language Models Transfer to Downstream Tasks?

record.file_problem: Minor text-extraction artifacts are present, but the full paper and appendices are included.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies model size, training data and compute, and measures held-out pre-training cross-entropy loss, though on chemical language models rather than general-purpose language models.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports downstream benchmark scores and per-task correlations. Rows below capture the main scaling outcomes and the explicit aggregate contrasts; detailed per-task scores and coefficients are noted under rows_left_out. Comparisons with prior models are not treated as scaling results for this study's models.
record.test_reason: The study pre-trains encoder chemical language models with MLM on SMILES while varying parameters, tokens and compute. It measures held-out pre-training loss, fits a Hoffmann-style power law, and measures downstream transfer on 36 MoleculeNet tasks. This is a new setting (molecular strings, masked LM) with direct results on V1, V5 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling resources consistently lowers CLM pre-training loss, but this does not reliably improve molecular-property transfer. Data and compute scaling in particular give limited benefit or negative transfer. They add that alternative proxies (Hessian trace, PGM distance) also fail, and they recommend task-aware evaluation.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies model size, training data and compute and measures held-out cross-entropy, but uses encoder-based masked language modeling on molecular strings. Its final-loss fit is a parameter-and-data function; it does not test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream outcomes vary by scaling axis, task and transfer protocol (fine-tuning versus linear probe). In the data-scaling experiment, gains at 0.7B to 2.7B tokens do not continue at 5.3B; in compute scaling, fine-tuning saturates early while linear-probe performance tends to deteriorate.

fits_no_version.finding: Hessian trace and PGM distance fail to predict downstream performance across checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-landscape proxies do not predict downstream transfer in chemical LMs.

record.problems: The scaling-law fit excludes the 0.7 and 1.3 billion-token conditions because training had not converged. The authors state that estimated exponents are not claimed to be universal. Downstream results vary by task and protocol; the paper reports three-seed standard deviations for downstream evaluations but does not report uncertainty for the fitted exponents.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed downstream results are reported separately for 36 tasks across model-, data- and compute-scaling figures and benchmark tables; Table 10 also gives per-task Spearman coefficients for fine-tuning and linear probe under each scaling axis. These task-level rows were not extracted individually; the main aggregate trends, explicit cross-task contrasts and the 26/36 compute-scaling result were prioritized.

untested.parts: Autoregressive natural-language pretraining. Data range is only ~1.2 orders of magnitude for the fit (2.7–42.4B tokens).
No extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal split.
Depth and width co-vary with size (Table 1); shape at fixed N is not varied.
Image, video, repeated-data and fine-tuning loss laws are not tested.
No comparison of exponents across fitting choices. The authors do note the fit is unstable when non-converged points are included, and that exponents exceed 0.5.

missing.what: MLM loss on downstream inputs (L_down) decreases monotonically with model size, data size and compute, matching L_pre.
Per-task Spearman coefficients by scaling axis. The compute-axis fine-tuning column appears mostly negative in the extracted text.
Per-task fine-tuning scores across the seven model sizes. Several QM8 tasks are non-monotonic in size (e.g. E1-CC2 best at 5.61M).
HIV ROC-AUC is non-monotonic over pre-training checkpoints while loss falls monotonically.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche is set to T3 rather than T1 because the domain (SMILES) and objective (masked LM) differ from the originals; the loss fit itself is Hoffmann-style. The fit excludes the 0.7B and 1.3B token conditions as non-converged. The fitted exponents (α=0.686, β=1.702) are unusually large, and the authors disclaim their universality; no uncertainty is given for them. Appendix F model sizes (0.25M–206.60M) appear to include embeddings, unlike Table 1. Peer-review status is not verifiable from the text.

versions.untested_parts: Autoregressive language modeling is not tested; the study uses masked language modeling. Its loss scaling is assessed only in the stated model, data and compute ranges.
The study does not fit laws on small runs and test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute sweep over parameter-count and token-count allocations, or compute-optimal split, is tested.
The study does not independently vary depth, width or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study tests chemical molecular-string models trained with MLM. It does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer as regimes for the pre-training loss law.
The study tests transfer to 36 molecular-property tasks under fine-tuning and linear-probe protocols; it does not test general language-model downstream tasks.
The paper describes fit choices and excludes non-converged data conditions, but does not compare fitted exponents across choices or test compute-optimal splits or curve bending away from a power law.
